title: Fireside Chat with Jeff Pintar on my lifetime Blackjack ban at a Vegas Casino on May 21, 2020
summary: A COVID-era webinar with real estate investor Jeff Pintar in which Pabrai argues the lockdowns have overreacted and damaged the economy for years, recounts his lifetime blackjack ban from a Vegas casino and the odds-based mindset behind it, and warns that FANG-led equity markets in May 2020 look like a broader bubble than 1999. He also contrasts Live Nation and Carriage Services to show how auction-driven pricing creates opportunity, explains the Buffett-partnership 0/6/25 fee structure and his decade without fees, and closes on Dakshana and why large inheritances are a disservice.

ideas.idea: The COVID lockdown was an overreaction that deliberately took a rockstar economy off the rails; the medicine is far worse than the disease.
ideas.detail: A three-week shutdown followed by contact tracing and distancing would have sufficed; nearly 40 million unemployment claims bring suicides, depression, divorce and abuse that nobody counts, and natural experiments in Sweden, Northern Italy and New York (20%+ already infected) argue against continued lockdown.

ideas.idea: Businesses are fragile; few can survive losing 60 or 90 days of revenue, so the shock will cause multiples of the normal 1,600 weekly US business failures and the economy will not be back to January 2020 levels even in five years.
ideas.detail: Normal creative destruction replaces 1,600 failures a week with better businesses; he expects unemployment to settle at 7-9% and says a 3% unemployment economy is unlikely even by 2025, though he would never bet against America or against Las Vegas as a town.

ideas.idea: He became a value investor by accident after reading Peter Lynch, which led him to Buffett and the idea that a stock is a fraction of a business to be analyzed as if buying the whole thing.
ideas.detail: Never went to business school; realized he could analyze businesses well and quickly using the same analytics as running a business, and started Pabrai Investment Funds in 1999 with $1 million as a hobby for friends.

ideas.idea: He received a lifetime blackjack ban from a Vegas casino on New Year's Eve 2019 because his non-card-counting system beat the house consistently.
ideas.detail: He visited every two or three months playing up to a few hundred dollars a hand and made a solid six figures; the casino had watched for over a year, could not find card counting, and said the trajectory plus the money behind him did not bode well for them.

ideas.idea: The first rule in blackjack, as in investing, is choosing which game and where to play so the odds are in your favor; he has zero interest in any bet where he lacks the edge.
ideas.detail: BJ21.com publishes the odds of every blackjack table in North America monthly for about $100 a year; blackjack is a fight for 50.1% versus 49.9%, whereas in equities he can make bets with 80% odds in his favor.

ideas.idea: You can optimize fun or optimize dollars, but not both.
ideas.detail: His friends find the way he plays blackjack extremely boring; he is all about optimizing dollars.

ideas.idea: In May 2020 the equity markets do not reflect economic reality and there is a bubble broader than the 1999-2000 one, because prices of FANG-type businesses are disconnected from any discounted cash flow.
ideas.detail: Nasdaq was flat on the year and the S&P down less than 15% while bargains were hard to find far above the March 23 lows; in 2000 the bubble was a sliver (Nasdaq 5,000 to 1,200), whereas today everything is built around a kernel of truth but every great business has a finite price.

ideas.idea: Microsoft in 2000 shows that a great business bought at an egregious price returns almost nothing: $600 billion market cap on under $10 billion of cash flow became about a 3% annual return over 21 years with a rough ride.
ideas.detail: He told Microsoft executives holding 80-90% of their net worth in the stock that it was going nowhere but down; it fell to less than a third and took 13-14 years to recover, reaching $1.3 trillion only by 2020.

ideas.idea: If long-term rates stay at 1-2% for years, equity markets and even FANG valuations are not expensive, but he cannot handicap rates with the printing presses running far beyond 2008-09.
ideas.detail: Fed and Treasury actions were the right thing and helped both Main Street and Wall Street, but they make 2008-09 look like nothing.

ideas.idea: Berkshire's actions in the crisis read as bearish: net sellers of equities, out of all airlines and Goldman Sachs, not buying back stock near book value, and Buffett saying $130 billion of cash is not that much.
ideas.detail: Munger described them as the captain of a ship in a tempest wanting to ride out the storm rather than roll the dice; Buffett had been willing to buy back Berkshire at 1.2x book before but was not buying now.

ideas.idea: Forget the macro; the micro always trumps the macro, and the investor's job is judging individual businesses, like a house bought for $250,000 with $25-30,000 of rent.
ideas.detail: It is not our job to figure out unemployment or interest rates; if the unlevered return from rent is known and the area is known, you do that deal all day long.

ideas.idea: He is an anomaly-based, bottom-up investor who never picks a sector first and then hunts for the best play within it.
ideas.detail: He always looks at what an individual business can do, and the same holds for real estate investors finding the mispriced house.

ideas.idea: Auction-driven markets produce strange pricing, which is the reason investors can make money in equities: Live Nation lost all 35,000 concerts but fell only about 40%, while Carriage Services fell 30% though its funeral business went up.
ideas.detail: A private funeral company worth $1 billion in January would laugh at a $700 million offer in April since revenues rose; funeral services has the lowest failure rate of any SIC code, people never shop quotes for a burial, and Live Nation's top line is gone for 2020 and most of 2021 yet its valuation was not compelling.

ideas.idea: The Buffett partnership 0/6/25 fee structure is the fair one: no management fee, a quarter of gains above 6%, and he went a decade (2007-2017) without a fee rather than resetting the high-water mark.
ideas.detail: A $5 billion fund charging 2% collects $100 million a year for breathing even when down 10%; he earned $30+ million in 2007, the funds fell about 65-67% by 2009, and he collected over $50 million in 2017-18 after regaining the high-water mark plus 6% a year. If the industry adopted this structure, 80% of it would disappear.

ideas.idea: Being far from financial epicenters like New York is an advantage because investing is a solitary activity of reading and thinking with less noise.
ideas.detail: Munger told Chris Davis that merely moving his operation from New York to Santa Barbara would add about half a percent a year to returns; Davis considered it but stayed.

ideas.idea: Large inheritances are a disservice to kids and grandkids, so the real answer is giving the money back to society efficiently, measured by social return on invested capital.
ideas.detail: Trust fund kids and welfare kids are both on an IV drip; he did not want to start thinking about giving in his seventies, so Dakshana was set up about 14 years earlier and got traction right away despite fears of corruption.

ideas.idea: Dakshana has taken on about 5,000 kids at roughly $3,000 each, with about 800 in the program at any time, preparing very poor students for IIT and medical entrance exams.
ideas.detail: Parents are mostly illiterate laborers earning under $100 a month; graduates work at Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Samsung, and one at Google earns over a quarter million a year while his father was a tailor making $50-60 a month. The 110-acre campus in Pune is on robust financial footing.
